summary: Extends the Layer Two Tunneling Protocol (L2TP) so it can carry Differentiated Services information. Before this, L2TP had no standard way to negotiate service differentiation for its control connection or its data sessions, so tunneled traffic could not be treated according to its priority class.

eli5.summary: A tunnel under a river treats every car the same. This document lets the tunnel know which cars are ambulances, so important traffic can be treated differently from ordinary traffic.

subtitle: How two L2TP peers agree on the forwarding treatment for a tunnel's control messages and for each session inside it.

tldr.problem: L2TP had no way to ask for Differentiated Services treatment, either for its control connection or for the individual data sessions inside a tunnel.
tldr.mechanism: Two new AVPs, CCDS (attribute 47) for the control connection and SDS (attribute 48) for a session, carry a 16-bit PHB code that the peers offer, accept or counter-offer during setup.
tldr.outcome: Each side maps the agreed PHB to a DSCP of its own DS domain and marks the outer IP header. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted.

today: RFC 3308 is a Proposed Standard published in November 2002, and no later RFC obsoletes or updates it. It builds on RFC 2661 for L2TP and on RFC 3140 for the PHB encoding.

sections.title: The Gap in L2TP
sections.content:
The Layer Two Tunneling Protocol (L2TP) tunnels PPP packets, but the L2TP specification (RFC 2661) has no mechanism for supporting Differentiated Services (diffserv, or DS). This document adds one so that L2TP can indicate the desired Per Hop Behavior (PHB) for the control connection and for individual sessions within a tunnel.

A PHB, as defined in RFC 2475, is the externally observable forwarding behavior a DS node applies to a particular behavior aggregate. The simplest example is guaranteeing a minimal bandwidth allocation of a link to that aggregate.

The RFC deliberately stays small. The actual bit interpretation of the DS field is out of scope; the document only defines a uniform exchange and a mapping mechanism for the new DS AVPs.
sections.eli5: L2TP could build a tunnel but could not say which traffic was more important. This document adds a way to say it.

sections.title: Negotiating for the Control Connection
sections.content:
The control connection runs in-band over the tunnel and handles setting up, maintaining and releasing the tunnel and its sessions. To give those control messages their own treatment, the RFC introduces the Control Connection DS (CCDS) AVP. Its presence in a Start-Control-Connection-Request (SCCRQ) tells the peer that the tunnel initiator wants both ends to use the PHB named by the AVP's PHB code for all packets of the control connection.

The terminator can respond in three ways:

  • If it does not support CCDS, it MUST ignore the AVP and send an SCCRP without it. The initiator reads the missing AVP as a lack of support.
  • If it supports CCDS, it SHOULD use the Host Name AVP from the SCCRQ to consult local policy. If it is unwilling or unable to use the requested code, it MUST send an SCCRP with a CCDS AVP holding the value it will use.
  • A matching value means acceptance; a different value is a counter-offer.

If the initiator does not want to continue after a missing or different answer, it sends a StopCCN carrying Result Code 8, which names the CCDS AVP (value 47) as the reason. If it still wants the tunnel after an SCCRP without CCDS, it sends an SCCCN.
sections.eli5: One side asks, 'Can we send our tunnel's own messages in the fast lane?' The other side says yes, offers a different lane, or says it does not know how. If the answer is no good, the first side can hang up.

sections.title: Negotiating for a Session
sections.content:
A session is created between the LAC and LNS when an end-to-end connection is established between a Remote System and the LNS. The Session DS (SDS) AVP lets the session initiator ask both ends to apply a PHB to all packets of that one session. It travels in ICRQ, ICRP, OCRQ and OCRP messages.

The flow mirrors the control connection, with a few differences. A terminator that provides no support for the requested PHB code MUST ignore the SDS AVP and reply without it. A terminator that supports SDS but is unwilling or unable to use the requested code MUST either send a CDN with Result Code 12, which names the SDS AVP (value 48), or reply with an SDS AVP holding the code it will accept. An initiator that gets no SDS AVP back may carry on with ordinary setup if it is willing to go without; otherwise it sends a CDN with Result Code 12. The same applies if it receives a different value that it will not use.

Because many sessions share one tunnel, the terminator needs a way to tell them apart when it checks policy. The initiator MAY use identifiers carried in the Proxy Authen Name, Calling Number, Called Number or Sub-Address AVPs, and the identifiers used SHOULD be configurable. The administrators of the LAC and LNS agree on this out of band.
sections.eli5: Inside the tunnel there can be many separate calls. Each call can ask for its own lane, and the other end can agree, offer something else, or end that call if the two cannot agree.

sections.title: The CCDS and SDS AVPs
sections.content:
Both AVPs use Vendor ID 0. The CCDS AVP has attribute type 47 and the SDS AVP has attribute type 48. Each is 8 octets long before hiding and ends in a 16-bit PHB Code field.

CCDS may appear in SCCRQ and SCCRP. SDS may appear in ICRQ, ICRP, OCRQ and OCRP. Both AVPs may be hidden (the H bit may be 0 or 1) and are optional, so the M bit is not set.

The two AVPs are independent. The PHB signaled in one SHOULD NOT have any implication for the other, implementations MAY support either or both, and operators may enable diffserv on either or both kinds of connection.
sections.eli5: Each request carries a tiny note with a lane code. There is one kind of note for the tunnel's own messages and another kind for each call.

sections.title: PHB Codes and DSCP Mapping
sections.content:
The PHB code is a left-justified 16-bit field using the PHB encoding defined in RFC 3140, which, along with its successor, is the ultimate authority on that encoding.

Once a control connection or session is established with the matching DS AVP, both LAC and LNS MUST use their own PHB-to-DSCP mappings for their present DS domains. They map the PHB to a DSCP and place it in the DS field of the outer IP header of packets sent on that connection. The rules for that mapping are set by administrative policy and are outside this document.

Signaling PHBs rather than DSCPs is deliberate. A connection may cross any number of DS domains, and a PHB keeps the end-to-end service consistent while each domain uses its own DSCP values. Boundary nodes may rewrite the DSCP, so it is acceptable for packets to arrive with an outer DS field different from the one the ingress node used (see RFC 2983).
sections.eli5: The two ends agree on what kind of treatment they want, not on a particular sticker. Each network then uses its own sticker for that treatment, so the meaning survives the trip even if the sticker changes.

sections.title: Reordering and Sequence Numbers
sections.content:
RFC 2474 recommends that PHB implementations not reorder packets within an individual connection, and RFC 3140 requires that a set of PHBs signaled with a single PHB ID must not cause additional reordering compared with a single PHB. Since the CCDS and SDS AVPs each carry one PHB ID, using them as specified should not add reordering within an L2TP control or data connection.

Control messages always carry sequence numbers for reliable delivery, so the chance of reordering with CCDS is the same as without it. Data messages MAY use sequence numbers to reorder packets and detect losses.
sections.eli5: Giving a car a lane should not shuffle the order of cars in the same line, and numbered tickets let the receiver fix any mix-up.

sections.title: IANA and Security Notes
sections.content:
IANA assigned AVP value 47 to CCDS and 48 to SDS. It also assigned L2TP Result Code 8 for disconnecting a control connection due to a mismatched CCDS value (StopCCN) and Result Code 12 for disconnecting a call due to a mismatched SDS value (CDN).

The encoding raises no security issues in itself. The RFC warns that modifying a DSCP may constitute theft or denial of service, so protocols using this encoding MUST be adequately protected. No new issues beyond those in RFC 2474 and RFC 2475 are introduced.
sections.eli5: If someone could secretly change the lane stickers, they could steal fast-lane service or jam it for others, so the tunnel needs protection.
